cards.grammarNote:
**은/는** marks the topic (**는** after a vowel, **은** after a consonant). **이에요/예요** = polite 'is/am/are' (**이에요** after a consonant, **예요** after a vowel):
**저는 학생이에요** (I'm a student). **저** = I (humble).

table.title: Particles change with the final sound
table.note: 학생은, 저는 · 눈이, 커피가 · 밥을, 커피를

cards.english: I eat rice. (object 을/를, verb last)
cards.grammarNote:
Korean is **Subject–Object–Verb** — the verb comes last. **을/를** marks the object (**을** after a consonant, **를** after a vowel):
**밥을 먹어요** (eat rice), **물을 마셔요** (drink water).

The **-요** ending makes speech polite but friendly — the everyday standard:
**먹어요** (eat), **가요** (go), **마셔요** (drink). Drop **요** for casual speech with close friends: **먹어**. **-ㅂ니다/습니다** is the formal ending.

produce.gloss: Add -아/어요 to the verb stem; dropped in casual speech.

cards.grammarNote:
**의** links owner to thing (A**의** B = 'A's B'). With **저** (I), **저의** usually shortens to **제**:
**제 이름** (my name), **제 친구** (my friend), **한국의 음식** (Korea's food).

cards.english: Are you a student? (same form, rising tone)
cards.grammarNote:
In polite **-요** speech, a yes/no question looks **identical to the statement** — only the rising intonation (and the '?') changes:
**학생이에요.** (You're a student.) → **학생이에요?** (Are you a student?). Nothing is added or reordered.

**주세요** = 'please give (me)' — the go-to way to order or request:
**물 주세요** (water, please), **커피 주세요** (a coffee, please). You can add the object particle **을/를**, but it's often dropped in speech.

produce.gloss: Polite way to ask for or order something.

cards.grammarNote:
**좋아해요** (to like) is a verb and takes the object particle **을/를**:
**커피를 좋아해요** (I like coffee), **과일을 좋아해요** (I like fruit). Don't confuse it with **좋아요** (it's good — an adjective).

Put **안** right before the verb to negate it:
**안 마셔요** (don't drink), **안 먹어요** (don't eat), **안 가요** (don't go). A more formal option is **-지 않아요**: **마시지 않아요**.

Korean adjectives conjugate like verbs and end the sentence directly — no separate 'is':
**맛있어요** (it's delicious), **매워요** (it's spicy), **뜨거워요** (it's hot). Just the adjective + **-요**.

produce.gloss: 맛있다 → 맛있어요. The -요 ending does the work.

cards.grammarNote:
**있어요** = there is / exists (also 'have'); the opposite is **없어요** (there isn't):
**은행이 있어요** (there's a bank), **화장실이 없어요** (there's no bathroom). The thing takes the subject particle **이/가**.

**에** marks a static location with **있어요** (to be/exist) — and also a destination with motion verbs:
**집에 있어요** (I'm at home), **학교에 가요** (I go to school). Read from the verb which meaning applies.
cards.englishPhrase: The bank is next to the school.

a.gloss: 에 = static location / destination (be at, go to)

cards.english: I eat at a restaurant. (place 에서 + action)
cards.grammarNote:
Use **에서** for where an action takes place (vs **에** for existence/destination):
**식당에서 먹어요** (eat at a restaurant), **집에서 일해요** (work at home). The action verb comes last.

cards.english: I go to the park. (destination 에 + 가요)
cards.grammarNote:
**에** + a motion verb (**가요** go, **와요** come) marks the destination:
**공원에 가요** (go to the park), **집에 가요** (go home). The verb comes last.
cards.englishPhrase: I'm going to the airport tomorrow.

cloze.prompt: I go to the park. (destination particle)

cards.grammarNote:
State a job with **저는 … 이에요/예요** (**예요** after a vowel, **이에요** after a consonant):
**저는 의사예요** (I'm a doctor), **저는 선생님이에요** (I'm a teacher). To ask: **무슨 일 하세요?** (what do you do?).

produce.gloss: 이에요 after a consonant, 예요 after a vowel (의사 → 예요).

cards.grammarNote:
**하다** (to do) → **해요** turns many nouns into verbs:
**운동해요** (exercise), **공부해요** (study), **요리해요** (cook), **일해요** (work). Very productive — attach **해요** to an activity noun.

produce.concept: noun + 해요 = to do (makes a verb)
produce.gloss: 공부해요 = I study, 일해요 = I work.

cards.english: I work at a company. (… 에서 일해요)
cards.grammarNote:
Use **에서** for the workplace + **일해요** (work):
**회사에서 일해요** (work at a company), **병원에서 일해요** (at a hospital). For 'work as a…', use the job + **(으)로**: **의사로 일해요**.

produce.concept: place + 에서 일해요 = to work AT a place
produce.task: say: I work at a company
produce.gloss: 에서 marks where the action happens.

cards.english: I like swimming. (verb + 는 것을 좋아해요)
cards.grammarNote:
To say you like *doing* something, turn the verb into a noun with **-는 것** + **을 좋아해요**:
**수영하는 것을 좋아해요** (I like swimming), **책 읽는 것을 좋아해요** (I like reading). **것** = 'thing / act'.

produce.concept: verb + 는 것을 좋아해요 = like doing
produce.answer: 수영하는 것을 좋아해요 suyeonghaneun geoseul joahaeyo
produce.gloss: 는 것 turns a verb into 'the act of ~'.

cards.grammarNote:
Emotion adjectives conjugate like verbs and end the sentence — no separate 'am':
**기뻐요** (I'm glad), **슬퍼요** (I'm sad), **행복해요** (I'm happy). The subject **저는** is usually dropped when it's clearly about you.

produce.concept: Feelings are adjectives that conjugate (no 'to be')
produce.gloss: 기쁘다 → 기뻐요. Just the -요 form.

cards.grammarNote:
Talk about mood with **기분** (feeling) + **이/가** + an adjective:
**기분이 좋아요** (I feel good), **기분이 나빠요** (I feel bad). Literally 'the feeling is good/bad'.
cards.englishPhrase: How do you feel? — I feel good.

produce.concept: 기분이 좋아요 = I feel good (lit. mood is good)
produce.gloss: 기분 = mood; 기분이 나빠요 = I feel bad.

cards.grammarNote:
Some feelings use **되다** (to become) → **돼요**, describing a state you've entered:
**긴장돼요** (I'm nervous), **걱정돼요** (I'm worried). It focuses on the feeling coming over you rather than a fixed trait.

produce.gloss: 긴장 (tension) + 돼요 = become nervous.

cards.grammarNote:
Many state words are **하다**-adjectives ending in **해요**:
**피곤해요** (I'm tired), **행복해요** (happy), **미안해요** (sorry). Add an adverb for degree: **너무 피곤해요** (I'm so tired).

produce.gloss: 피곤하다 → 피곤해요. Same 해요 pattern.

cards.grammarNote:
To say a body part hurts, mark it with **이/가** + **아파요** (to hurt / be sick):
**머리가 아파요** (headache), **배가 아파요** (stomachache), **목이 아파요** (sore throat). **아프다** conjugates like an adjective.

Show possession with **제** (my, from 저의) before the body part:
**제 손** (my hand), **제 눈** (my eyes). In everyday speech Koreans often drop it when it's obvious whose body part it is.

produce.gloss: 제 comes from 저의. 제 이름 = my name.

cards.grammarNote:
**이/가** marks the subject — the thing being described (**이** after a consonant, **가** after a vowel):
**눈이 커요** (the eyes are big), **손이 작아요** (the hands are small). Add a topic for 'I have…': **저는 눈이 커요**.

Korean adjectives end the sentence themselves — no separate 'are':
**손이 차가워요** (hands are cold), **손이 따뜻해요** (hands are warm). Add a topic for whose: **저는 손이 차가워요** (my hands are cold).

produce.gloss: 손이 (hands) + 차가워요 (are cold). The adjective conjugates.

cards.grammarNote:
Strip **다** from the dictionary form to get the stem. If the last vowel is ㅏ or ㅗ, add **아요**; otherwise add **어요**:
**먹다** → 먹 + **어요** = **먹어요**. **가다** → 가 + **아요** = **가요** (contracted).

table.title: 아요 vs 어요 — last vowel rule
table.note: 마시다 contracts: 마시 + 어요 → 마셔요

cards.grammarNote:
**가다** (to go) has stem **가** — last vowel ㅏ → add **아요**, but **가 + 아요** contracts to **가요**.
**오다** (to come) stem **오** (ㅗ vowel) → **오 + 아요** = **와요**.

produce.concept: 가다 and 오다 contract with 아요
produce.gloss: 가 + 아요 → 가요 (contracted); 오 + 아요 → 와요

cards.grammarNote:
When the stem ends in **이**, it merges with **어요** → **여요** (then often written as **셔요**):
**마시다** → 마시 + 어요 → **마셔요** (drink). Same pattern: **보이다** → 보여요.
cards.englishPhrase: I drink coffee at the cafe.

cards.grammarNote:
**하다** is special: **하 + 여요** → **해요** (irregular contraction).
Thousands of compound verbs use **하다**: **공부해요** (study), **운동해요** (exercise), **요리해요** (cook), **일해요** (work).

table.title: 하다 verbs → 해요
table.note: 하 + 여요 → 해요 — always irregular

cards.grammarNote:
Korean has two main polite registers:
**해요체** (haeyo-che): everyday polite → **먹어요, 가요, 해요**
**합쇼체** (hapsho-che): formal → **먹습니다, 갑니다, 합니다** — used in speeches, news, military, work reports.

contrast.prompt: Everyday polite vs formal speech level

cards.grammarNote:
**반말** (banmal) = casual speech — drop **요** from 해요 forms:
**먹어요** → **먹어**, **가요** → **가**, **해요** → **해**. Only use with close friends, younger people, or children. Never with elders or new acquaintances.

a.gloss: polite — drop 요 to get casual

cards.english: 있어요 (there is) vs 없어요 (there is not)
cards.grammarNote:
**있다** (to exist/have) → **있어요**; **없다** (to not exist/lack) → **없어요**.
Both are adjective-verbs: **화장실이 있어요** (there's a bathroom), **화장실이 없어요** (there's no bathroom).

cloze.prompt: There is a bank here. (existence verb)

cards.grammarNote:
**살다** (to live) has stem **살** — last vowel ㅏ → **살 + 아요** = **살아요** (no contraction since stem ends in consonant ㄹ, not a vowel).
Contrast: **가다** (stem 가, ends in vowel) contracts to **가요**.

table.title: 살다, 먹다, 공부하다 — conjugation
table.note: 살 ends in consonant ㄹ — no contraction; vowel-final stems contract

cards.grammarNote:
Add **(으)세요** to the verb stem to make a polite request or mild command:
**앉다** (sit) → **앉으세요** (please sit), **가다** → **가세요** (please go), **드세요** (please eat — honorific).
**(으)** appears when the stem ends in a consonant.

produce.gloss: 기다리 (vowel-final) + 세요; 앉 (consonant-final) + 으세요

cards.grammarNote:
Attach **고 싶어요** to the verb stem to express a wish:
**먹고 싶어요** (I want to eat), **가고 싶어요** (I want to go), **마시고 싶어요** (I want to drink). The stem never changes.

**-고 있어요** = progressive aspect (action in progress):
**먹고 있어요** (I'm eating), **공부하고 있어요** (I'm studying). Built from **-고** (connective) + **있어요** (to exist/be).

produce.answer: 지금 공부하고 있어요 jigeum gongbuhago isseoyo
produce.gloss: 공부하 + 고 있어요 → 공부하고 있어요

cards.grammarNote:
Formal speech ending: **습니다** after a consonant stem, **ㅂ니다** after a vowel stem:
**먹다** → 먹**습니다**, **가다** → 갑**니다**, **하다** → 합**니다**. Used in announcements, presentations, military, and formal work settings.

table.title: Formal -ㅂ/습니다 endings
table.note: Questions: 먹습니까? / 갑니까? — add 까 for formal questions

cards.grammarNote:
In formal speech, questions use **-ㅂ니까? / 습니까?** instead of a rising tone:
**갑니까?** (Are you going?), **먹습니까?** (Are you eating?). Polite casual just uses rising intonation: **가요?**

**이에요** after a consonant-final noun; **예요** after a vowel-final noun:
**학생이에요** (is a student — 생 ends in consonant), **의사예요** (is a doctor — 사 ends in vowel). Formal: **학생입니다**.

cloze.prompt: I am a doctor. (vowel-final noun 의사)

cards.grammarNote:
Drop **요** from 해요 forms for casual 반말 with close friends:
**먹어요** → **먹어**, **가요** → **가**, **공부해요** → **공부해**, **있어요** → **있어**. For **이에요/예요** → **이야/야**.
cards.englishPhrase: Are you okay? (to a close friend)

table.title: 해요 → 반말 (drop 요)
table.note: Only use 반말 with close friends, children, or younger people

cards.grammarNote:
Past tense mirrors the vowel rule: **ㅏ/ㅗ** → **았어요**; other → **었어요**:
**가다** → 갔어요, **먹다** → 먹었어요, **하다** → 했어요. Add -요 for polite speech.
cards.englishPhrase: I ate rice at the restaurant.

table.title: Past tense — 았어요 / 었어요 / 했어요
table.note: 가 + 았어요 → 갔어요 (contracted); 하 + 였어요 → 했어요

cards.grammarNote:
**가다** (go): 가 + 았어요 → 갔어요 (the two vowels merge). Common error is **가었어요** — the contraction **갔어요** is required.
Question: **어디 갔어요?** (Where did you go?)
cards.englishPhrase: I went to the hospital yesterday.

cards.grammarNote:
**하다** (do) → 했어요 (irregular contraction). All **하다** compound verbs use the same pattern:
**공부했어요** (studied), **운동했어요** (exercised), **요리했어요** (cooked), **일했어요** (worked).
cards.englishPhrase: I studied at the library yesterday.

produce.gloss: 하다 always contracts → 했어요 in the past

cards.grammarNote:
**살다** (live): stem **살** (ㅏ vowel) → **살 + 았어요** = **살았어요**.
**마시다** (drink): stem **마시** (이 vowel) → **마시 + 었어요** → contracts to **마셨어요**.

Past tense questions are identical to statements — only the rising intonation and '?' differ:
**밥 먹었어요.** (I ate.) → **밥 먹었어요?** (Did you eat?). This parallels the present-tense question rule.
cards.englishPhrase: Did you go to work today?

cards.grammarNote:
**ㄹ/을 거예요** expresses future intention or plan:
**먹을 거예요** (I'll eat / going to eat), **갈 거예요** (will go), **할 거예요** (will do). Use **ㄹ** after vowel stems, **을** after consonant stems.
cards.englishPhrase: I'm going to eat at the restaurant.

table.title: ㄹ/을 거예요 — future
table.note: 거예요 contracts → 거에요 is also acceptable in speech

cards.english: 갈 거예요 — will go (vowel stem + ㄹ)
cards.grammarNote:
**가다** stem is **가** (vowel-final) → add **ㄹ 거예요** directly: **갈 거예요**.
Contrast with consonant stem **먹다** → **먹을 거예요** (the filler vowel 으 is inserted).
cards.englishPhrase: I will go to the park tomorrow.

cloze.prompt: I will go to school tomorrow. (future)

cards.grammarNote:
**겠** expresses speaker's will, strong intention, or polite conjecture (what you're about to do):
**먹겠어요** (I will eat / I'm going to eat — assertive), **감사하겠습니다** (I will be grateful — polite).
Less common in casual speech; often sounds formal or literary.

Time adverbs go at the START of a sentence (before subject or topic):
**어제** (yesterday), **오늘** (today), **내일** (tomorrow). They do not change form and require no particle.
cards.englishPhrase: Yesterday I went to the store. Tomorrow I will rest.
cards.phrase: 어제 가게에 갔어요. 내일은 쉴 거예요.
cards.phraseRomanized: Eoje gagee gasseoyo. Naeireun swil geoyeyo.

table.title: Core time adverbs
table.note: Place at the front: 어제 먹었어요 / 오늘 먹어요 / 내일 먹을 거예요

cards.english: 었어요 vs 을 거예요 — past vs future drill
cards.grammarNote:
Quick contrast of the three main tenses:
**먹었어요** (ate — past), **먹어요** (eat — present), **먹을 거예요** (will eat — future).
cards.englishPhrase: Yesterday I ate, today I'm eating, tomorrow I will eat.
cards.phrase: 어제 먹었어요, 오늘 먹어요, 내일 먹을 거예요.
cards.phraseRomanized: Eoje meogeosseoyo, oneul meogeoyo, naeil meogeul geoyeyo.

table.title: Three tenses with 먹다
table.note: Same pattern works with 가다: 갔어요 / 가요 / 갈 거예요

cards.grammarNote:
Past tense of **고 싶어요** (want to): **고 싶었어요**.
**먹고 싶었어요** (I wanted to eat), **가고 싶었어요** (I wanted to go). The verb stem stays unchanged; only 싶다 goes past.

produce.task: say: I wanted to go to the park
produce.answer: 공원에 가고 싶었어요 gongwone gago sipeosseoyo
produce.gloss: 가 + 고 싶었어요 — 싶다 → 싶었어요 (past)

cards.grammarNote:
Simple past with a destination: **집에 갔어요** (went home). Note **집에** = to/at home (destination 에 + 가다 past).
Contrast: **집에 있어요** (I'm at home — present state).

**하다** stem **하** (vowel-final) → **할 거예요**:
**공부할 거예요** (will study), **운동할 거예요** (will exercise), **요리할 거예요** (will cook). The ㄹ attaches directly to the vowel-final stem.

produce.task: say: I will study and cook tomorrow
produce.gloss: 하 (vowel) + ㄹ 거예요 → 할 거예요

cards.grammarNote:
Korean is Subject–Object–Verb. The tense marker sits inside the verb at the END:
**저는** (S) **밥을** (O) **먹었어요** (V-past). Adverbs go before the subject or after it: **어제 저는 밥을 먹었어요**.
cards.englishPhrase: Yesterday I ate rice at the restaurant.

table.title: Korean sentence order (past)
table.note: Verb always last; tense is inside the verb ending

cards.grammarNote:
Korean particles are postpositions glued to nouns that show their role in the sentence:
**은/는** = topic, **이/가** = subject, **을/를** = object. The choice between the two forms in each pair depends on whether the noun ends in a consonant or a vowel.

table.title: Core particles — consonant vs vowel final
table.note: 학생은, 저는 · 눈이, 커피가 · 밥을, 커피를

cards.grammarNote:
**은** after a consonant-final noun; **는** after a vowel-final noun:
**저는** (I — topic; 저 ends in vowel → 는), **학생은** (student — topic; 생 ends in consonant → 은).
cards.englishPhrase: As for me, I eat rice.

cards.grammarNote:
**이** after a consonant-final noun; **가** after a vowel-final noun:
**커피가** (coffee — subject; 피 ends in vowel → 가), **눈이** (eyes — subject; 눈 ends in ㄴ → 이).

**을** after a consonant-final noun; **를** after a vowel-final noun:
**밥을** (rice — object; 밥 ends in ㅂ → 을), **커피를** (coffee — object; 피 ends in vowel → 를).

**에** marks a static location (with **있어요**) or a destination (with motion verbs like **가요/와요**):
**학교에 있어요** (I'm at school), **학교에 가요** (I go to school). 에 attaches directly, no consonant/vowel variation.

produce.task: say: I'm at the hospital / I go to the hospital
produce.gloss: 에 is invariant — no consonant/vowel split

cards.grammarNote:
**에서** = where an action takes place (vs. **에** for static existence or destination):
**식당에서 먹어요** (eat at a restaurant), **도서관에서 공부해요** (study at the library).

a.gloss: 에 = static location (be at / go to)

cards.grammarNote:
**도** replaces **은/는, 이/가, 을/를** to mean 'also / too':
**저도** (me too), **커피도** (coffee too), **학교도** (school too). When emphasizing the verb, use **도** after the verb: not the noun.

**로** (after vowel or ㄹ) / **으로** (after other consonants) marks means of transport, direction, or role:
**버스로** (by bus), **왼쪽으로** (to the left), **의사로 일해요** (work as a doctor).

table.title: 로 / 으로 — usage and forms
table.note: 로 = way/direction/role; not the same as 에 (destination)

cards.grammarNote:
In casual or fast speech, particles — especially **을/를** and **이/가** — are often dropped:
**커피 마셔요** (drink coffee), **학교 가요** (go to school). **은/는** is dropped less often, and **에/에서** almost never dropped.

**에** also marks points in time (hours, days, years):
**아침에** (in the morning), **오전에** (in the morning / at AM time), **내일에** is unnatural — 내일 alone works for 'tomorrow'. Note: **오늘/어제/내일** do not take 에.

table.title: 에 for time vs place
table.note: 오늘/어제/내일 do NOT take 에 — use bare word

cards.english: 에 vs 에서 — choose the right particle
cards.grammarNote:
Quick rule: **에** = WHERE something IS or WHERE you GO TO; **에서** = WHERE an ACTION happens.
**카페에 있어요** (I'm at the cafe), **카페에서 공부해요** (I study at the cafe).

cloze.prompt: I study at the library. (action particle)

cards.grammarNote:
Full sentence with all three core particles:
**저는** (I — topic은), **커피를** (coffee — object를), **마셔요** (drink). SOV order confirmed.
cards.englishPhrase: I drink coffee at the cafe.

produce.task: say: I eat rice at the restaurant
produce.answer: 저는 식당에서 밥을 먹어요 jeoneun sikdangeseo babeul meogeoyo
produce.gloss: 저는(topic) 식당에서(action-place) 밥을(object) 먹어요(verb)

cards.grammarNote:
**도** fully replaces 은/는 or 이/가 (not added on top):
**저도** (not 저는도), **커피도** (not 커피가도). For 을/를: **커피도 마셔요** (I also drink coffee — 도 replaces 를).

cloze.prompt: I go to school too. (도 after place particle 에)

cards.grammarNote:
**에서** also marks ORIGIN (from a place) with verbs of departure or source:
**한국에서 왔어요** (I came from Korea), **서울에서 왔어요** (came from Seoul). Context (come/go vs. do something) clarifies meaning.

a.gloss: 에서 = where the action happens (at school)

cards.grammarNote:
With motion verbs **가다** (go) and **오다** (come), **에** marks the destination:
**공원에 가요** (go to the park), **집에 와요** (come home). Compare: **공원에서 운동해요** (exercise in the park).
cards.englishPhrase: I go to the park on weekends.

cloze.prompt: I go to the park. (destination particle)

cards.english: 은/는 (topic) vs 이/가 (subject) — the big picture
cards.grammarNote:
**은/는** (topic) = 'as for …' — sets the frame, often contrasts, or introduces shared info.
**이/가** (subject) = identifies WHO or WHAT does the action or has the property, often new info.
Both can appear in the same sentence: **저는 커피가 좋아요** (As for me, it's coffee I like).
cards.englishPhrase: As for me, coffee is what I like.

a.gloss: topic: 'as for …' — frame, contrast, shared info

b.gloss: subject: new info, identifies the doer

cards.grammarNote:
Use **이/가** when introducing NEW information — the listener doesn't know what you're about to identify:
**Q: 뭐가 맛있어요?** (What is delicious?) **A: 커피가 맛있어요** (Coffee is delicious — 커피 is the new, identified answer).
cards.englishPhrase: Q: What's delicious? A: The coffee is delicious.

cloze.prompt: What's delicious? Coffee is. (new info → subject particle)

cards.grammarNote:
**은/는** sets a topic and everything that follows is ABOUT that topic:
**저는 학생이에요** = 'As for me, I'm a student.' The topic is often the speaker (저는) or something just mentioned.
cards.englishPhrase: As for me, I'm a student.

produce.concept: 은/는 frames the topic — 'as for X, ...'
produce.task: say: As for me, I work at a company.
produce.answer: 저는 회사에서 일해요 jeoneun hoesaeseo ilhaeyo
produce.gloss: 저는 sets the topic (I); everything after is about the speaker

cards.grammarNote:
**은/는** implies contrast — 'this one (but not the other)':
**커피는 좋아요, 차는 싫어해요** (I like coffee, but I don't like tea). If there's no contrast intended, **이/가** is more neutral.
cards.englishPhrase: I like coffee, but I don't like tea.

contrast.prompt: 은/는 signals contrast between two items

cards.english: 저는 + 이/가 in the same sentence
cards.grammarNote:
Both can appear together: **저는** (topic = 'as for me') + **커피가** (subject = coffee is identified as what I like):
**저는 커피가 좋아요** — literally 'As for me, coffee is likable.' This is how Koreans say 'I like coffee' — coffee takes **이/가**.
cards.englishPhrase: I like coffee. (lit. As for me, coffee is good.)

table.title: 저는 커피가 좋아요 — double particle
table.note: 좋아요 is an adjective — coffee is the subject, not the object

cards.english: 이/가 to identify the ONE who does something
cards.grammarNote:
When YOU are the one doing something (emphasis, identification, or answering '누가?'), use **제가** (I + subject) not **저는**:
**Q: 누가 했어요?** (Who did it?) **A: 제가 했어요.** (I did — subject, not topic).
cards.englishPhrase: Q: Who did it? A: I did.

cloze.prompt: I did it. (identifying yourself as doer → subject particle)

cards.grammarNote:
**은/는** is used when the topic is already known to both speakers or was just mentioned:
**A: 학교가 어디예요?** (Where is the school?) → **B: 학교는 저기예요** (The school is over there — 학교 is now known/shared topic).

a.gloss: 이/가 — new question, school not yet in context

b.gloss: 은/는 — school is now the shared topic

cards.grammarNote:
In Korean, the topic (and subject) is frequently DROPPED when context is clear:
**밥 먹었어요?** (Have you eaten? — subject 당신은 implied). The particles are also often dropped in casual speech.

contrast.prompt: Full form vs. naturally dropped topic

a.term: 당신은 밥을 먹었어요? dangsin-eun babeul meogeosseoyo?

cards.grammarNote:
**저는 슬퍼요** = 'As for me, I'm sad' — general statement about myself.
**제가 슬퍼요** = 'I'm the one who is sad' — identifies the speaker; may imply others are not, or is an answer to '누가 슬퍼요?'
cards.englishPhrase: As for me, I'm sad. / I'm the one who's sad.

contrast.prompt: 저는 vs 제가 — topic vs subject (I)

a.gloss: topic — general 'as for me, I'm sad'

b.gloss: subject — I'm the specific one who is sad

cards.grammarNote:
**물이 맛있어요** — new info: 'It's the WATER that's delicious' (identifies water as the thing).
**물은 맛있어요** — topic/contrast: 'As for water, it's delicious' (implies other things may not be).

cloze.prompt: Neutral new info: 'The coffee is delicious.' (no contrast intended)

cards.grammarNote:
**은/는** is used for general/universal statements — what is GENERALLY true about a topic:
**음식은 맛있어요** (Food is delicious — in general). This is similar to the English 'Food is good' meaning generally.

produce.concept: 은/는 for general truths about a topic
produce.task: say: Water is good / Water is delicious (generally)
produce.gloss: 은/는 = general claim about the topic (water in general)

cards.grammarNote: **누구** (who) + **가** (subject particle) = **누가** (who — as subject): **누가 해요?** (Who does it?), **누가 왔어요?** (Who came?). The question word takes **이/가**, not **은/는**.

cards.english: Same word, different particle = different meaning
cards.grammarNote:
**학교가 좋아요** — new focus: 'It's the SCHOOL that's good' (e.g., as an answer to what's good).
**학교는 좋아요** — topic/contrast: 'As for school, it's good' (possibly: but something else isn't).
cards.englishPhrase: It's school that's good. / As for school, it's good.

contrast.prompt: 이/가 vs 은/는 on the same noun

a.gloss: 이/가 — new info: SCHOOL is the good thing

cards.grammarNote:
In relative/embedded clauses, the subject inside the clause takes **이/가** (not **은/는**):
**제가 좋아하는 음식** (the food that I like — 제가 is the subject of the embedded clause 좋아하는). **은/는** cannot mark subject in a clause.
cards.englishPhrase: The food that I like is delicious.

produce.concept: 이/가 marks subject in embedded clauses (not 은/는)
produce.task: say: the food that I eat (내가 먹는 음식)
produce.answer: 제가 먹는 음식 jega meongneun eumsik
produce.gloss: 제가 = subject inside the clause; 음식 = the modified noun

cards.grammarNote:
Rules of thumb:
1. NEW info → **이/가**. Known/shared topic → **은/는**.
2. CONTRAST between items → **은/는**.
3. Embedded clause subject → **이/가**.
4. General truth → **은/는**.
cards.englishPhrase: I like coffee. The coffee is delicious.

table.title: 은/는 vs 이/가 — decision rules
table.note: Both can appear in one sentence: 저는(topic) 커피가(new subj) 좋아요

cards.grammarNote:
Korean marks social respect grammatically. Three tools:
1. **(으)시** infix in the verb — the SUBJECT is respected
2. **께서** — honorific subject particle (replaces 이/가)
3. **Special honorific verbs** — 드리다, 계시다, 잡수시다, 주무시다

table.title: Honorific tools in Korean
table.note: Honorifics refer to the SUBJECT being respected, not the listener

cards.grammarNote:
Add **(으)시** to the verb stem to honor the SUBJECT of the sentence:
**가다** → 가 + **시** + 어요 = **가세요** (goes — honorific). **으시** is used when the stem ends in a consonant: **앉다** → 앉**으시**어요 → **앉으세요**.

table.title: (으)시 — adding the honorific infix
table.note: Vowel stem: + 세요 directly; consonant stem: + 으세요

cards.grammarNote:
When the verb stem ends in a CONSONANT, insert **으** before **시**:
**앉다** (sit) → 앉 + **으시** + 어요 = **앉으세요** (please sit — honorific/polite command). Compare: **읽다** → **읽으세요** (please read).

**께서** replaces **이/가** when the SUBJECT deserves respect:
**선생님께서 오세요** (The teacher is coming — honorific). In practice, **이/가** is also used with honorific verbs and is acceptable; **께서** is more formal.

**계시다** is the honorific replacement for **있다** (to be/exist):
**선생님이 계세요** (The teacher is here — honorific). Never use **있어요** when the subject is someone you respect.

a.term: 제 친구가 있어요 je chinguga isseoyo

cards.grammarNote:
**드리다** = honorific of **주다** (to give) — use when the RECEIVER of the giving is someone you respect:
**선생님께 드려요** (I give [it] to the teacher). **드리다** → 드려요 (present), 드렸어요 (past).
cards.englishPhrase: I give it to the teacher.

a.gloss: 주다 → 줘요 — give to a friend (plain)

cards.grammarNote:
**께** is the honorific indirect object marker (replaces **에게** / **한테**):
**친구에게 줘요** → **선생님께 드려요** (give to the teacher). Use **께** when the recipient is a respected person.
cards.englishPhrase: Please give this to the teacher.

table.title: Indirect object particles — plain vs honorific
table.note: 한테 is most common in casual speech; 에게 is more formal/written

cards.grammarNote:
**주무시다** = honorific of **자다** (to sleep):
**안녕히 주무세요** (Good night — 'sleep peacefully' to an elder). **잘 자요** is the casual equivalent for friends.

a.gloss: 자다 → 자요 — plain (to a close friend)

cards.english: 잡수시다 / 드세요 — to eat (honorific of 먹다)
cards.grammarNote:
**먹다** (eat) has two honorific replacements:
**드시다** → **드세요** (more common, slightly formal): '드세요, 많이 드세요' (please eat / eat a lot).
**잡수시다** → **잡수세요** (very formal, traditional).

table.title: 먹다 honorific replacements
table.note: 드세요 is most common at the dinner table with elders

cards.grammarNote: **하다** → **하세요** (honorific). Very common in: **어떻게 하세요?** (How do you do? — polite greeting), **무슨 일 하세요?** (What do you do for work? — polite inquiry).
cards.englishPhrase: What do you do for work?

produce.task: say: What do you do for work? (politely)
produce.answer: 무슨 일 하세요? museun il haseyo?
produce.gloss: 하 + 시 + 어요 = 하세요. Polite question to a stranger.

cards.grammarNote:
Koreans use a HUMBLE form of 'I' when speaking to someone of higher status:
**저** = humble 'I' (with elders, strangers, formal contexts), **나** = plain 'I' (casual friends). This is part of the broader system of raising others and lowering yourself.

cards.english: 가요 vs 가세요 — plain vs honorific verb
cards.grammarNote:
**가요** = plain polite (speaker or peer goes); **가세요** = honorific (respected person goes OR polite request 'please go').
Context: **선생님이 가세요** (the teacher is going) vs. **어서 오세요** (please come in — polite welcome).
cards.englishPhrase: The teacher is going. / Please go.

cloze.prompt: The teacher is going. (honorific verb for respected subject)

cards.english: Title 님 — the universal honorific suffix
cards.grammarNote:
**님** is added to titles and names as an honorific suffix:
**선생님** (teacher — honored), **의사 선생님** (doctor — honored). Adding **님** to a name: **Jeff님**. Also: **사장님** (CEO/boss), **손님** (customer/guest — honored).

produce.task: say: The teacher is here (honorific verb: 계시다)
produce.gloss: 선생님 = teacher + 님; 계세요 = honorific 있어요

cards.grammarNote:
Key honorific verb replacements:
**먹다 → 드시다**, **있다 → 계시다**, **자다 → 주무시다**, **주다 → 드리다**, **말하다 → 말씀하시다**. These replace the plain verb entirely when the subject is honored.
cards.englishPhrase: The teacher is eating. The teacher is sleeping.

table.title: Plain → Honorific verb pairs
table.note: 드리다 lowers the giver; 계시다/드시다/주무시다 raise the subject

cards.grammarNote:
Place **안** directly BEFORE the verb to negate:
**안 먹어요** (don't eat), **안 가요** (don't go), **안 마셔요** (don't drink). Short negation is the most common spoken form.

**못** goes before the verb to express INABILITY (can't) — either physical or circumstantial:
**못 먹어요** (can't eat), **못 가요** (can't go). Compare: **안 먹어요** = don't eat (choice), **못 먹어요** = can't eat (unable).
cards.englishPhrase: I can't go to work today.

cards.grammarNote:
**-지 않아요** = long-form negation; more formal/written than **안 + verb**:
**먹지 않아요** (do not eat), **가지 않아요** (do not go), **마시지 않아요** (do not drink). Past: **먹지 않았어요**.

contrast.prompt: Short 안 vs long 지 않아요 negation

cards.grammarNote:
**-지 못해요** = long-form inability; parallels **-지 않아요** for negation:
**가지 못해요** (cannot go), **먹지 못해요** (cannot eat). Often used in formal contexts or for emphasis.
cards.englishPhrase: I cannot go to the hospital today.

contrast.prompt: Short 못 vs long 지 못해요

cards.english: 하다 verbs + 안: 안 해요 (not 안공부해요)
cards.grammarNote:
With **하다** compound verbs, **안** goes between the noun and **해요**:
**공부 안 해요** (don't study — correct), NOT 안 공부해요 (unnatural).
**운동 안 해요** (don't exercise), **요리 안 해요** (don't cook).

**없어요** (from 없다) = 'there isn't' or 'I don't have' — not a negated verb, but an independent negative adjective:
**화장실이 없어요** (there's no bathroom), **돈이 없어요** (I don't have money). Opposite: **있어요**.

Korean adjectives conjugate like verbs, so **안** negates them too:
**안 맛있어요** (not delicious), **안 피곤해요** (not tired), **안 바빠요** (not busy). Works the same as verbal negation.

Past negation: **안** stays before the verb, and the verb takes the past ending:
**안 먹었어요** (didn't eat), **안 갔어요** (didn't go), **안 했어요** (didn't do). The **안** position doesn't change.
cards.englishPhrase: I didn't eat at the restaurant.

produce.answer: 어제 공부 안 했어요 eoje gongbu an haesseoyo
produce.gloss: 안 goes before 해요 → 안 했어요 in past

cards.grammarNote:
Past inability: **못** before past verb:
**못 갔어요** (couldn't go), **못 먹었어요** (couldn't eat), **운동 못 했어요** (couldn't exercise). Same position as present **못**.
cards.englishPhrase: I couldn't go to school yesterday.

cloze.prompt: I couldn't work yesterday. (past inability, 하다 verb)

cards.grammarNote:
To negate a NOUN predicate (X이에요/예요), use **아니에요** (is not):
**학생이에요?** — **아니에요, 선생님이에요** (Not a student — a teacher). **아니에요** is a separate word and replaces **이에요/예요** entirely.
cards.englishPhrase: I'm not a student, I'm a teacher.

cards.english: 안 vs 못 — choosing the right negation
cards.grammarNote:
Use **안** for choice/will ('don't want to / choose not to') and **못** for inability ('can't / not possible'):
**고기를 안 먹어요** (I don't eat meat — vegetarian by choice), **오늘 못 가요** (I can't go today — something prevents me).
cards.englishPhrase: I don't eat meat (by choice). / I can't eat meat (allergy).
cards.phrase: 고기를 안 먹어요. / 고기를 못 먹어요.
cards.phraseRomanized: Gogireul an meogeoyo. / Gogireul mot meogeoyo.

produce.task: How do you say 'I can't drink coffee' (unable)?
produce.answer: 커피를 못 마셔요 keopireul mot masyeoyo
produce.gloss: 못 = inability; 안 마셔요 = choose not to drink

cards.english: 먹지 않았어요 — did not eat (long past negation)
cards.grammarNote:
Long-form past negation: **verb + 지 않았어요**:
**먹지 않았어요** (did not eat), **가지 않았어요** (did not go). The past tense is on **않다**: 않았어요.
cards.englishPhrase: I did not go to work yesterday.

cloze.prompt: I did not eat. (long-form past negation)

cards.grammarNote:
Four negation patterns:
1. **안** + verb (short won't)
2. **못** + verb (short can't)
3. verb + **지 않아요** (long won't — formal)
4. verb + **지 못해요** (long can't — formal)
cards.englishPhrase: I don't eat / I can't eat / I do not eat / I cannot eat.
cards.phrase: 안 먹어요 / 못 먹어요 / 먹지 않아요 / 먹지 못해요.
cards.phraseRomanized: An meogeoyo / mot meogeoyo / meokji anayo / meokji motaeyo.

table.title: Korean negation patterns
table.note: 안/못 go before verb; 지 않다/지 못하다 attach to verb stem

cards.grammarNote:
**-고** connects two verb phrases: V1 + **고** + V2 (do A and then B, or A and B together):
**먹고 가요** (I eat and then go), **공부하고 자요** (I study and sleep). The subject doesn't change between clauses.
cards.englishPhrase: I eat and go to school.

produce.concept: V + 고 = and then / and also
produce.gloss: 운동하 + 고 + 먹어요 — tense goes on the LAST verb only

cards.english: -고 — tense only on the last verb
cards.grammarNote:
In **-고** chains, ONLY the final verb carries tense:
**공부하고 자요** (study and sleep), **공부하고 잤어요** (studied and slept — the whole sequence is past). Don't put past tense on each verb.

cloze.prompt: I ate and went. (tense on last verb only)

cards.grammarNote:
**-아서/어서** connects a CAUSE (V1) to a RESULT (V2) — 'because' or 'so':
**배가 고파서 먹어요** (I'm hungry so I eat). Vowel rule same as 아요/어요:
**고프다** → 고파서, **먹다** → 먹어서. NO past tense on the first verb.

table.title: -아서/어서 formation
table.note: Tense goes on the LAST verb, not on 아서/어서 clause

cards.grammarNote:
**아서/어서** can also mean 'go/do A and then do B' (tight sequence where V1 enables V2):
**가서 먹어요** (go and eat), **만나서 이야기해요** (meet and talk). Use **-고** for looser listing; **-아/어서** for tighter cause or sequence.
cards.englishPhrase: I go to the restaurant and eat.

a.gloss: -고 = loose and/then (eat, then go — two actions)

cards.grammarNote:
**(으)니까** expresses a reason the SPEAKER is asserting — often used when giving a justification or suggestion:
**피곤하니까 쉬어요** (Since I'm tired, I'll rest). Unlike **아서**, **니까** CAN take past tense: **갔으니까**.

a.gloss: 아서 — natural cause/result; NO 아서 in commands

b.gloss: 니까 — assertive reason; OK in commands/suggestions

cards.grammarNote:
**-아서/어서** CANNOT be followed by commands or suggestions — use **-(으)니까** instead:
**피곤하니까 쉬세요** (Since you're tired, please rest — 니까 + command OK).
**피곤해서 쉬세요** = WRONG in formal grammar.
cards.englishPhrase: Since it's delicious, please eat a lot.

cloze.prompt: Since it's delicious, please eat. (니까 for command context)

cards.grammarNote:
**-지만** = 'but / although' — connects a concession to a contrasting result:
**비싸지만 맛있어요** (It's expensive, but delicious), **피곤하지만 일해요** (I'm tired, but I work). Attaches directly to the verb/adj stem.

produce.task: say: I'm tired, but I exercise
produce.gloss: 피곤하 + 지만 + 운동해요 — stem + 지만 (no vowel alternation)

cards.grammarNote:
**지만** can combine with past tense on V1:
**먹었지만 배고파요** (I ate, but I'm still hungry). The verb before **지만** carries its own tense normally.
cards.englishPhrase: I studied, but I don't understand.

cloze.prompt: I studied but don't understand. (past + 지만)

cards.grammarNote:
**-는데** (verb) / **-은데/ㄴ데** (adjective) provides background context or a soft contrast:
**음식이 맛있는데 가격이 비싸요** (The food is delicious, but the price is expensive). Also used to introduce a topic: **저 지금 바쁜데요…** (I'm busy right now, but...).
cards.englishPhrase: The food is delicious, but the price is expensive.

table.title: -는데 / -은데 forms
table.note: 는데 softens the contrast; 지만 is more direct. Both mean 'but'.

cards.english: 지만 vs 는데 — direct vs soft contrast
cards.grammarNote:
**지만** = direct, clear opposition ('but').
**는데 / 은데** = softer, background-setting ('though / and yet'). In speech, **는데** is more common and flexible; **지만** sounds more deliberate.
cards.englishPhrase: It's expensive but good. (direct vs soft)

b.gloss: 는데 — softer, backgrounding (more natural in speech)

cards.english: 아서/어서 vs 니까 — which to use?
cards.grammarNote:
Key difference:
**아서** = natural, observable cause; cannot precede commands.
**니까** = stated/assertive reason; CAN precede commands and suggestions.
cards.englishPhrase: Since it's delicious, I eat a lot. / Since it's delicious, eat a lot!
cards.phrase: 맛있어서 많이 먹어요. / 맛있으니까 많이 드세요.
cards.phraseRomanized: Masisseo mani meogeoyo. / Masisseunnikka mani deuseyo.

produce.concept: 아서 = natural reason; 니까 = stated reason (ok with commands)
produce.task: Which is correct: 피곤해서 쉬세요 or 피곤하니까 쉬세요?
produce.gloss: 니까 before commands: OK. 아서 before commands: ungrammatical.

cards.grammarNote:
**-고** = simple list ('and'): **밥 먹고 가요** (eat rice and go — two actions).
**-아서/어서** = cause or tight sequence: **식당에 가서 먹어요** (go to the restaurant in order to eat). Choose based on whether the relationship is causal/sequential or just additive.
cards.englishPhrase: I eat and go. / I go (and then) eat.
cards.phrase: 밥 먹고 가요. / 식당에 가서 먹어요.
cards.phraseRomanized: Bab meokgo gayo. / Sikdange gaseo meogeoyo.

cloze.prompt: I'm hungry so I eat. (cause → result)

cards.english: 는데요 — polite topic intro / soft disagreement
cards.grammarNote:
**-는데요** at the end of a sentence introduces a topic, gives background, or softly hints at disagreement:
**지금 바쁜데요** (I'm busy right now…) — implies 'so what do you want / that's difficult'. Very common in conversational Korean.
cards.englishPhrase: I'm busy right now… (hint of unavailability)

contrast.prompt: 는데요 as a polite soft hint

b.gloss: soft hint: I'm busy (so... / it's difficult)

cards.grammarNote:
**-고** = and/then (additive)
**-아서/어서** = because / in order to (cause, sequence; no commands)
**-(으)니까** = because/since (justification; OK with commands)
**-지만** = but (direct contrast)
**-는데** = but/though (soft, background)
cards.englishPhrase: I eat rice and go. / I'm tired so I rest. / It's expensive but good.
cards.phrase: 밥 먹고 가요. / 피곤해서 쉬어요. / 비싸지만 좋아요.
cards.phraseRomanized: Bab meokgo gayo. / Pigonhaeseo swieoyo. / Bissajiman joayo.

cards.grammarNote:
Korean has several irregular classes where the stem changes before vowel endings:
**ㅂ** (돕다), **ㄷ** (듣다), **ㅅ** (낫다), **르** (모르다), **ㅎ** (빨갛다), **ㄹ** (알다 — the regular-seeming one). Each class has its own rule.

table.title: Irregular classes in Korean
table.note: Regular: 먹다 → 먹어요 (no change); irregulars change the stem

cards.english: ㅂ irregular — ㅂ becomes 우/오 before vowels
cards.grammarNote:
ㅂ-irregular verbs: when **ㅂ** is the final consonant and a VOWEL follows, **ㅂ** changes to **우** (or **오** in 돕다/고맙다):
**돕다** (help) → 도 + 와요 = **도와요**; **고맙다** (grateful) → 고마 + 워요 = **고마워요**.

table.title: ㅂ irregular — present and past
table.note: ㅂ → 와 (after ㅗ vowel) or 워 (after other vowels)

cards.grammarNote:
**돕다** (to help): ㅂ stem. Before **아요**, ㅂ → 와: 도 + 와요 = **도와요**.
**도움** (help) is a known noun; the verb **돕다** is the irregular.

cards.english: ㄷ irregular — ㄷ becomes ㄹ before vowels
cards.grammarNote:
ㄷ-irregular verbs: **ㄷ** becomes **ㄹ** before a vowel ending:
**듣다** (hear/listen) → 들 + 어요 = **들어요**. Before consonants, ㄷ stays: **듣고** (听-and). Regular exception: **받다** (receive) is regular → **받아요**.

table.title: ㄷ irregular — 듣다
table.note: 받다 (receive) looks similar but is REGULAR: 받아요

cards.grammarNote:
**듣다** (listen): ㄷ stem. Before **어요**, ㄷ → ㄹ: 들 + 어요 = **들어요**.
**들었어요** (past — heard). **듣고** (and listen — consonant, no change).
cards.englishPhrase: I listen to music every day.

cards.english: ㅅ irregular — ㅅ drops before vowels
cards.grammarNote:
ㅅ-irregular verbs: **ㅅ** DROPS before a vowel ending:
**낫다** (to get better) → 나 + 아요 = **나아요** (get better). Regular exception: **씻다** (wash) is regular → **씻어요** (washes).

table.title: ㅅ irregular — 낫다
table.note: 씻다 (wash) looks similar but is REGULAR: 씻어요

cards.grammarNote:
**르** verbs: the 르 syllable splits — the ㄹ moves to the previous syllable:
**모르다** (not know) → 몰라요, **부르다** (call) → 불러요. Pattern: stem vowel + ㄹ + 라/러요.

table.title: 르 irregular pattern
table.note: 르 → (prev syllable)ㄹ + 라/러요; NOT 르아요

cards.grammarNote:
**모르다** (not know): 모 + 르 → 몰 + 라요 = **몰라요**.
Past: 몰랐어요. With **고** (consonant): 모르고 (and not know — no change).

cards.english: ㅎ irregular — ㅎ drops + vowel changes
cards.grammarNote:
ㅎ-irregular adjectives: **ㅎ** drops before a vowel, and the preceding vowel changes:
**빨갛다** (red) → 빨개요 (stems in ㅏ/ㅗ + ㅎ → 애, others → 에). This class is almost entirely colors/states.

table.title: ㅎ irregular adjectives
table.note: ㅎ drops before 아/어; the preceding vowel merges → 애/에

cards.english: ㄹ 'irregular' — ㄹ drops before ㄴ, ㅂ, 시, 오
cards.grammarNote:
ㄹ verbs are often called 'irregular': **ㄹ** drops before **ㄴ, ㅂ, 시, 오**:
**알다** (know) → **알아요** (before vowel, no drop), **아는** (knowing — ㄹ dropped before ㄴ), **압니다** (formal — ㄹ dropped before ㅂ), **아세요** (honorific — ㄹ dropped before 시).

table.title: 알다 (know) — ㄹ irregular
table.note: Before VOWELS: ㄹ stays. Before ㄴ/ㅂ/시/오: ㄹ drops

cards.grammarNote: **살다** (to live): same ㄹ pattern as **알다** — **살아요** (before vowel), **사는** (drop before ㄴ), **삽니다** (formal), **사세요** (honorific).

produce.task: Give: present / formal / honorific for 살다
produce.gloss: 살아요 (vowel→keep ㄹ), 삽니다 (ㅂ→drop ㄹ), 사세요 (시→drop ㄹ)

cards.grammarNote:
Not every verb is irregular:
**받다** (receive) looks like a ㄷ verb but is REGULAR → **받아요** (not 발아요).
**씻다** (wash) looks ㅅ irregular but is REGULAR → **씻어요** (not 씻아요 / 씨어요). You have to memorize which are truly irregular.
cards.englishPhrase: I receive / I wash / I listen.

cards.grammarNote:
Memory hook for all 6 classes:
**ㅂ** → 우/와 (돕→도와), **ㄷ** → ㄹ (듣→들어), **ㅅ** drops (낫→나아), **르** → ㄹㄹ (모르→몰라), **ㅎ** drops+vowel-merge (빨갛→빨개), **ㄹ** drops before ㄴ/ㅂ/시 (알→아세요).
cards.englishPhrase: All irregular classes at a glance.
cards.phrase: 도와요 / 들어요 / 나아요 / 몰라요 / 빨개요 / 알아요.
cards.phraseRomanized: Dowayo / deoreoyo / naayo / mollayo / ppalgaeyo / arayo.

table.note: Learn the irregular class for each verb when you first encounter it
